document_check.note: Guo Y, Pai M, Xue B, Lu W. 'Bidirectional association between depressive symptoms and mild cognitive impairment over 20 years: Evidence from the Health and Retirement Study in the United States', Journal of Affective Disorders 338 (2023) 449-458, doi 10.1016/j.jad.2023.06.046. Read in full to the reference list (pages 1-9, journal pp. 449-457). Design (HRS 1998 sub-cohort, competing-risks regression), the Ns (9317 and 9428) and the cited SHRs 1.20 (1.08-1.34) and 1.16 (1.01-1.33) all appear in the document.

cited_result: Principal: the fully adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio for baseline high-risk depressive symptoms (CES-D-8 at or above 4) and incident MCI, SHR 1.20 (95% CI 1.08-1.34), N=9317. Reverse direction: baseline MCI and incident high-risk depressive symptoms, SHR 1.16 (1.01-1.33), N=9428 (Tables 2 and 3, pp. 4-6). Also cited: the continuous-score multilevel growth-curve sensitivity analysis (p. 4).
tool_reason: The cited result is a longitudinal association between a baseline condition (high-risk depressive symptoms, and reciprocally MCI) and a later incident outcome in a population cohort, estimated by covariate-adjusted competing-risks regression without a causal-estimation design (no propensity scores, weighting or target-trial emulation), so under clarification 1 of 2026-09-29, and the operator's tool review of this record, the JBI cohort checklist applies rather than ROBINS-E.

domains.domain: Item 1: Were the two groups similar and recruited from the same population?
domains.rationale: Exposed and unexposed participants come from the same source: the 1998 HRS baseline sample, with the same inclusion and exclusion rules for everyone. Baseline characteristics are reported only for the whole analytic sample, not by exposure group (Table 1), so how similar the groups were is not shown. Differences between them are handled by adjustment (items 4 and 5).

signalling.question: 1. Were the two groups similar and recruited from the same population?
signalling.quote: We set 1998 as the study baseline and tracked the risk of outcome in these baseline participants over the following 20 years. This study therefore included the sub-cohort in 1998 only. ... A sample of 20,012 core participants at baseline was obtained by excluding those who did not respond at the baseline interview, had died or were living in a nursing home (baseline weight = 0). ... In the analytic sample for subsequent MCI, 12.0 % of participants had baseline high-risk depressive symptoms.

domains.domain: Item 2: Were the exposures measured similarly to assign people to both exposed and unexposed groups?
domains.rationale: Every participant's exposure was assigned from the same instrument at the same 1998 wave: the CES-D-8 with a single cut-off, or, in the reverse direction, the composite cognitive score.

signalling.question: 2. Were the exposures measured similarly to assign people to both exposed and unexposed groups?
signalling.quote: High-risk depressive symptoms are indicated when the total score is ≥4 (Mojtabai and Olfson, 2004). We used binary variables for high-risk depressive symptoms as the outcome (subsequent high-risk depressive symptoms) and the primary exposure (baseline high-risk depressive symptoms), respectively.

domains.domain: Item 3: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domains.rationale: The exposure is measured with a published short form of the CES-D, using a cut-off from the literature that the HRS team has endorsed. Its limits are that it is a single baseline screening measurement, not a diagnosis, and it does not capture change in exposure over 20 years.

signalling.question: 3. Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: the specificity and sensitivity of these cut-offs for the CES-D (≥4 to define high-risk depressive symptoms) and cognitive scores (7–11 to define MCI) have been developed, assessed, and endorsed by the HRS team itself (Crimmins et al., 2011; Steffick, 2000).

domains.rationale: A literature-based set of baseline confounders is named: sociodemographic factors, wealth, father's education, lifestyle, BMI and long-term conditions. Four plausible confounders are not in it: the baseline cognitive score within the normal range (12-27), the baseline CES-D score below the cut-off for the reverse direction, antidepressant use and genetic risk. The authors acknowledge that residual confounding is possible (p. 8). The item asks whether confounders were identified, and a substantive set was, so the answer is Yes, with the omission recorded.

signalling.question: 4. Were confounding factors identified?
signalling.quote: baseline variables (1998, Wave 4) including age (years), gender (Male; Female), race (White/Caucasian; Black/African American; Other), marital status ..., education ..., total household wealth ($), father with 8+ years of education (Yes; No), smoking ..., physical activity (Yes; No), BMI (Normal weight; Pre-obesity; Obesity), and long-term conditions (Yes; No) were considered to be covariates.

domains.domain: Item 5: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domains.rationale: The strategy is stated: multivariable adjustment in competing-risks models, reported as unadjusted, minimally adjusted and fully adjusted. A sensitivity model leaves out covariates that might be mediators.

signalling.question: 5. Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
signalling.quote: The minimally adjusted model controlled for age and gender. The fully adjusted model additionally controlled for other covariates. ... Second, intermediate models were developed without adjusting for behavioral variables (smoking, alcohol consumption, physical activity, and BMI) and marital status, as they might be influenced by depression and/or cognition.

domains.domain: Item 6: Were the participants free of the outcome at the start of the study?
domains.rationale: People who already had the outcome at baseline were excluded: MCI or dementia (composite score 0-11) for the principal direction, high-risk depressive symptoms for the reverse direction.

signalling.question: 6. Were the groups/participants free of the outcome at the start of the study (or at the moment of exposure)?
signalling.quote: We further excluded samples who already reported outcome of interest (MCI/dementia; high-risk depressive symptoms) at baseline

domains.domain: Item 7: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domains.rationale: Incident MCI is classified from a published, interviewer-administered composite of cognitive performance tests with standard HRS cut-offs, applied the same way to everyone, so the instrument is objective and has a validation pedigree. Three things leave its reliability here unclear. First, a single wave below the cut-off counts as incident MCI, with no confirmation and no allowance for reversion (4296 incident cases among 9317). Second, the text contradicts itself on later dementia-range scores: participants scoring in that range at subsequent visits 'have been excluded', yet the outcome coding counts subsequent dementia as MCI, with onset imputed at the midpoint. Third, nothing is reported on interviewer training or proxy respondents. The authors call MCI measurement 'an unresolved issue'. In the reverse direction the outcome is a self-reported CES-D-8 at or above 4 at a single wave.

signalling.question: 7. Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
signalling.quote: MCI is measured by a composite cognitive score (0–27) developed using HRS data (Crimmins et al., 2011). ... When the total scores were between 0–6, 7–11 and 12–27, participants were considered to have dementia, MCI without dementia, and normal respectively (Crimmins et al., 2011). ... At subsequent visits, those participants who scored in the ‘dementia’ range have been excluded. ... The measurement criteria for MCI remains an unresolved issue (Petersen et al., 2014).

domains.domain: Item 8: Was the follow-up time reported and sufficient for outcomes to occur?
domains.rationale: Follow-up ran up to 20 years (1998-2018), with a mean of 11.0 years for the principal analysis, which is long enough for incident MCI to occur.

signalling.question: 8. Was the follow up time reported and sufficient to be long enough for outcomes to occur?
signalling.quote: Thus, this study used HRS data over a 20-year period (1998–2018; Waves 4–14). ... For the association between baseline high-risk depressive symptoms and subsequent MCI (N = 9317), 4296 incident cases of MCI and 1910 competing events were identified; and 3111 participants were right censored. The mean year of follow-up was 11.0 years

domains.domain: Item 9: Was follow-up complete, and if not, were the reasons for loss described and explored?
domains.rationale: Follow-up was not complete. Participants with missing outcome data across waves were excluded from the analysis, and the analytic samples (9317 and 9428) are well under half of the 20,012 baseline core participants. The main text does not say how many were lost for this reason or why; it refers to Supplements I and II, which were not available. The authors did compare excluded and analysed participants: excluded participants more often had the exposure at baseline and had less education. The exploration is reported qualitatively in the main text, with the detail only in Supplement IV.

signalling.question: 9. Was follow up complete, and if not, were the reasons to loss to follow up described and explored?
signalling.quote: missing data on continuous outcome measures across waves before the end of follow-up (see Supplements I and II for detailed explanation) ... In both investigations, excluded participants tended to have baseline exposures, less problematic drinking, lower household income, normal weight, lower education level, vigorous physical activity, long-term conditions, and fathers with less than eight years of education and be male, Black/African American and current smoker compared to analytic participants (see Supplement IV). ... Second, selection bias may exist due to attrition and non-responsiveness.

domains.domain: Item 10: Were strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilised?
domains.rationale: Participants with missing outcome data across waves were excluded rather than kept and censored at their last observation. Multiple imputation covered only missing baseline exposure and covariates, not incomplete outcome follow-up. No weighting for attrition is reported. The imputation sensitivity analysis therefore does not address the loss to follow-up.

signalling.question: 10. Were strategies to address incomplete follow up utilised?
signalling.quote: Third, we performed multiple imputation using chained equations to deal with missing data for baseline depressive symptoms/MCI and covariates.

domains.domain: Item 11: Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
domains.rationale: Fine-Gray competing-risks regression, with death as the competing event and SHRs with 95% CIs, suits a time-to-event outcome in an older cohort with substantial mortality (1910 competing events). Adjustment is described, and effect modification was tested. The paper reports no check of the proportional subdistribution hazards assumption, and event times are taken as the interview month at detection (interval censoring ignored). These are minor reporting gaps, not an inappropriate method. Complete-case exclusion is assessed under item 10.

signalling.question: 11. Was appropriate statistical analysis used?
signalling.quote: Competing-risks regression was applied. Participants were divided into three groups. In the first investigation, 0 = censored – by the end of follow-up the participant was still alive and had never experienced subsequent MCI; 1 = subsequent MCI; and 2 = other competing events – the participant died without a subsequent MCI occurring ... Sub-distribution hazard ratios (SHRs) with 95 % confidence intervals (CI) were calculated.

overall_rationale: By the review's rule for this checklist, none of items 4, 5, 7 or 11 is No, so the rating is not high. Not every applicable item is Yes: outcome reliability is unclear (item 7), follow-up was incomplete and the loss is described only through supplements (item 9), and nothing addressed incomplete follow-up (item 10). The rating is therefore some concerns. The main threats to this result are the exclusion of participants with incomplete outcome follow-up, who were more often exposed, and a single-wave threshold definition of incident MCI.
